primary_claim: The orthogonality and polytope structures reported for categorical/hierarchical concept representations in LLMs (Park et al. ICML 2024; Jiang et al. ICML 2024) occur practically everywhere, including for semantically opposite concepts, totally random/nonsensical concepts, and even random untrained unembeddings, indicating the results are a generic artifact of the whitening transformation and high dimensionality rather than evidence of meaningful learned geometry.

effect.metric: orthogonality / convex-hull (polytope) formation of whitened concept probes
effect.value: semantically opposite and random-nonsense concept sets show the same near-orthogonality and simplex/polytope formation as hierarchical concept sets; effect reproduces even with a random, untrained unembedding matrix

contradicts_or_qualifies: Challenges the interpretation of Park et al. (ICML 2024, arXiv:2406.01506) and the Linear Representation Hypothesis paper (arXiv:2311.03658) that observed orthogonality/polytope structure reflects meaningful categorical/hierarchical concept geometry learned by the model
stated_future_work: A framework unifying how representations are obtained (contrastive activations, PCA, SAE, etc.), how they're used by the model, and how they can be used to control it (e.g. steering vectors)
How to determine how well a given direction/vector/function represents a given human-interpretable concept
If orthogonality and simplices are too universal, what is a good lens or theory for studying the geometry of categorical and hierarchical concepts
Using a coloring transformation (inverse of whitening, learned directly from data) instead of the whitening transformation
quote: The main takeaway is that the orthogonality and polytopes they observe in categorical and hierarchical concepts occur practically everywhere, even at places they should not.
